title: The Epic Your Sons Need You to Live
author: Catholic Manhood
summary: Nick from Catholic Manhood reads Homer's Odyssey as a Catholic father's manual, arguing that the poem is not primarily an adventure story but a story about a father's relentless fight to return home to his family. He draws particular attention to the often-skipped 'Telemachy', the first four books that follow Odysseus's son Telemachus, arguing that Telemachus's passivity illustrates how a father's absence shapes his children just as powerfully as his presence would, and that one can be home in body but absent in formation. Odysseus's refusal of every temptation (Calypso's immortality, the Sirens' knowledge, the Lotus Eaters' comfort) is reframed as the daily Catholic calling to resist the offers that would end the journey home. The article closes with five lessons for fathers, insisting that what disqualifies a father is not struggle but surrender.
points: The Odyssey is fundamentally a story about fatherhood: Odysseus endures twenty years of hardship not for glory but to return to Penelope and Telemachus.
The Telemachy (Books 1-4) shows that a father's absence actively forms his children; Telemachus's passivity is the product of having no man to model courage.
Every temptation in the poem is a version of the same offer, 'stop going home,' making the poem a mirror for modern fathers facing comfort and distraction.
A father can be physically present yet absent in formation; children need active engagement in shaping who they become, not merely a body in the house.
What disqualifies a father is not struggle or failure but surrender; Odysseus is a model because he never stopped trying to return.
quotes: But the Odyssey is not primarily an adventure story. It is truly about a father attempting to get home to his family.
All of the temptations in the poem are but a version of the same offer: stop going home.
A father's absence forms children just as much as his presence does. This shape, or lack thereof, is pressed into a man's children whether or not he intends it or is aware of it.
Telemachus is passive because that is all he has ever known. Men who should have filled that gap failed. No one was forming him.
What disqualifies a father is not struggle. It is surrender, and that is much worse.
